content: Chromium deficiency is a medical condition that arises due to an insufficient intake of dietary chromium. This condition is uncommon in developed countries. Trivalent chromium is an essential trace element required for the proper metabolism of glucose in humans. In contrast, hexavalent chromium is highly toxic and mutagenic. Trivalent chromium is a critical component of the glucose tolerance factor (GTF), a metalloprotein complex. GTF is formed when the oligopeptide chromodulin, which consists of the amino acids aspartate, cysteine, glutamate, and glycine, binds with four trivalent chromium (Cr3+) ions. Recent research indicates that this metalloprotein plays a significant role in enhancing insulin receptor activity, thereby improving insulin efficiency. The recommended daily intake of chromium for adults has been revised to 30–35 µg for males and 20–25 µg for females, down from the previous range of 50–200 µg. Only about 2% of ingested trivalent chromium is absorbed by the body, with the remainder excreted in feces. The absorption of chromium can be enhanced by vitamin C and niacin. Once absorbed, chromium is stored in the liver, bones, and spleen for future use. Factors such as a diet high in simple sugars or fats, infections, pregnancy, lactation, or acute physical exercise can reduce chromium levels in the body. Chromium is excreted primarily through urine. Due to its low absorption rate and high excretion rate, chromium toxicity is rare, even with supplementation. Chromium deficiency can manifest through a variety of symptoms, including elevated blood cholesterol levels, impaired glucose metabolism, fatigue, increased plaque accumulation in the aorta, hypertension, anxiety, stunted physical growth in children, delayed wound healing, atherosclerosis, reduced glucose tolerance, and potentially decreased fertility and lifespan. Chromium picolinate is the most commonly used synthetic supplement to address chromium deficiency and correct glucose metabolism imbalances. This compound enters cells via a different mechanism than naturally occurring trivalent chromium in food. For chromium to be utilized within cells, it must be released from chromium picolinate through a process that reduces the chromic center, which may generate harmful hydroxyl radicals. The safety of chromium picolinate supplementation remains a topic of debate. However, studies have shown its effectiveness in patients receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN), and it is routinely added to TPN solutions. Trivalent chromium is naturally present in a variety of foods, which can help meet dietary chromium requirements and address deficiencies. These foods include egg yolks, whole-grain products, high-bran breakfast cereals, coffee, nuts, green beans, broccoli, meat, brewer’s yeast, and certain brands of wine and beer.
